title: Lie down
subtitle: The next step after learning to sit
objective: Teach the dog to lie down on the command “down”, holding the position for several seconds.
why: Calms the dog during exciting moments
Helps control situations in public spaces
benefits: Your dog will relax in restaurants, terraces or long visits
Ideal posture for prolonged rest and barking control
Foundation to teach “stay” for several minutes
Reduces reactivity: a dog lying down doesn't jump or lunge
where: 🏠 At home (comfortable floor, rug or living room)
⛔ Avoid cold, hard or slippery surfaces at first
beforeYouStart: Your dog must already know “sit” fluently
Make sure the surface is comfortable (no cold floor)
Train after a short walk: a slightly tired dog learns better
Have at least 15 small treats ready

methods.title: L-shaped lure method (recommended)
methods.description: You guide the dog with a treat tracing an L: first downward between their paws, then forward.
methods.bestFor: Puppies and dogs that already know sit

steps.title: Starting position: sit
steps.description: Ask your dog to sit. This is the ideal starting point because the hips are already lowered.
steps.tip: If they don't respond fluently to sit, go back to that course first.
steps.troubleshooting: If they break the sit, calmly ask again without scolding.

steps.title: Downward motion
steps.description: Place the treat on their nose and slowly lower it to the floor between their front paws.
steps.troubleshooting: If they stand up, ask for sit again and restart slower.

steps.title: Forward motion
steps.description: Once the treat is on the floor, slide it forward in a straight line. The dog will stretch and lie down.
steps.tip: The full motion traces a capital L.

steps.title: Introduce the command
steps.description: Once fully lying (belly touching the floor), say clearly: “down”.
steps.tip: Only say the word when fully lying, not halfway.

steps.title: Reward and reinforce
steps.description: Give the treat immediately, on the floor between their paws. Praise with happy voice.
steps.tip: Rewarding on the floor reinforces the position and prevents standing.

steps.title: Increase duration
steps.description: When done on first try, wait 1 second before rewarding. Build to 3, 5, 10 seconds gradually.
steps.tip: If they break the position early, drop back to the previous duration.

methods.title: Raised platform method
methods.description: You use a low step or cushion: the dog is half-elevated, making it easier for front paws to slide forward.
methods.bestFor: Large dogs, anxious dogs, or those that don't respond to lure

steps.title: Place dog on a low cushion
steps.description: A 5–10 cm tall platform. Firm cushion, low step or yoga block.
steps.tip: The front edge must be free.

steps.title: Ask for sit on the platform
steps.description: The dog should sit on the cushion. Reward.
steps.tip: If uncomfortable on it, spend a few minutes familiarizing them.

steps.title: Lure forward
steps.description: Lure their front paws forward (off the platform). They'll naturally fall into the down position.
steps.tip: The trick: the elevated platform makes lying down physically easier.

steps.title: Mark and reward
steps.description: Once fully down, say “down” and reward.
steps.tip: Repeat until they associate the word.

steps.title: Remove the platform
steps.description: After 5–10 sessions with platform, try on flat ground. Should work the same.
steps.tip: If not, return to the platform 2–3 more sessions.

commonErrors.error: Pushing the dog down with your hand on the back
commonErrors.cause: Frustration when the lure doesn't work first try
commonErrors.fix: Never use physical force. Improve the lure motion or use the platform method.
Wait until belly and elbows are on the floor before rewarding. Otherwise you reinforce intermediate positions.

commonErrors.error: Practicing on cold or slippery surfaces
commonErrors.fix: Always use rug, bed or carpet. Dogs instinctively avoid lying on cold/hard surfaces.
Fluent “sit” is a prerequisite. If not mastered, don't ask for down yet.

troubleshooting.problem: Follows the treat with nose but doesn't lower body
troubleshooting.solution: You're moving the treat too fast or too far. Keep it stuck to the floor and move very slowly forward.

troubleshooting.problem: Lies down but stands up immediately
troubleshooting.solution: Normal at first. Reward faster (within 1 second) and gradually increase duration.

troubleshooting.problem: Does a “sphinx” pose but doesn't lie laterally
troubleshooting.solution: Sphinx is valid and sufficient. Lateral form is more relaxed but not required for the basic command.
May be joint pain. Consult the vet. Meanwhile, use a very padded surface.

progressMilestones.goal: Follows treat to the floor and bends front legs
Fully lies down with the lure 60% of attempts
Lies down on “down” command without needing the lure
Holds the position 30 seconds before reward

successSigns: Lies down on command with no visible lure
Does it in different places and positions
Holds the position more than 10 seconds
Returns to lying if they break the position when asked again
variations: Full lateral down (on side, not sphinx)
Down during your breakfast while you eat
Down with only a downward hand gesture
Down after a chained sit (combining commands)
safetyNotes: If your dog shows pain or cracking when lying, consult the vet before continuing
Large breeds (Mastiffs, Great Danes) may take longer due to anatomy
Never force physically: it can create fear and command rejection
Puppies under 14 weeks: max 3 minutes per session
funFact: Dogs only lie laterally (on their side) when they feel 100% safe. If yours does this with you, it's a sign of deep trust.
nextLevel: Increase duration to 1–2 minutes. Practice with distractions and in public. Then introduce “stay”.
proTip: If your dog won't lie, go back to “sit” and repeat slower. Always toss the treat to the floor between paws, never hand-feed: this reinforces staying down.
